title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

title: CreditFilter: Calibrated Token Weights over the Within-Response Entropy Rank for RLVR
abstract: Critic-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically assigns a uniform advantage to every token. Token-reweighting heuristics like the 80/20 mask favor high-entropy tokens, but fail to measure a token's actual impact on the outcome. We formalize this impact as the forking value: the variance of the success probability over the policy's next-token choices. The expected forking values along a response sum exactly to the reward variance. Token credit is thus, in expectation over a prompt's responses, a fixed budget spent at the forks. This motivates weights that redistribute credit within a response. The forking value factorizes into a fork consequence, which requires costly continuations to estimate, and a fork probability, which the softmax provides. On Qwen3-8B-Base, this fork probability decays exponentially with a token's within-response entropy rank at class-specific rates, revealing that most tokens carry negligible forking value. CreditFilter weights each token by an exponential window over the same rank. The window is calibrated to this fork-probability envelope, under an approximately flat fork consequence. CreditFilter needs no extra forward passes and is stabilized by difficulty damping and an entropy-gated fallback. Averaged over three seeds, it outperforms DAPO by 7.7 points on MATH500 and by 10.5 and 9.1 points on AIME24 and AIME25. Its dynamically adaptive variant matches it. The ablations show that both parts matter: ranking tokens within each response rather than across the batch, and matching the window's decay rate to the envelope. Code is available at https://github.com/yoctta/CreditFilter.

title: Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced Hierarchy-Aware Semi-Supervised Graph Classification
abstract: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the issue of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.

title: NoiseRater: Meta-Learned Noise Valuation for Diffusion Model Training
ss_tldr: NoiseRater is introduced, a network that scores an individual noise instance conditioned on the data sample and timestep, and its properties establish instance-level noise valuation as a new axis for understanding and improving diffusion training.
abstract: Training a diffusion model involves two sources of randomness for each data sample: the timestep and the Gaussian noise realization. The timestep has been studied extensively through scheduling and weighting, whereas the impact of the noise realization at a given timestep is still underexplored. In this work, we examine whether different noise instances are equally informative. We introduce NoiseRater, a network that scores an individual noise instance conditioned on the data sample and timestep. The rater is learned through bilevel optimization, where its scores reweight the diffusion loss in the inner loop, and it is updated to reduce validation loss after the inner-loop updates. Using the trained rater to select training noise, we observe three properties of training noise. First, noise realizations at the same timestep are not equally useful: the rater's top-scored noise improves performance over i.i.d. sampling, while its bottom-scored noise degrades it. Second, this utility is contextual: it depends most strongly on the timestep, and to a lesser extent on the image and the class label. Third, noise selection is complementary to timestep-level design, retaining most of its gain when combined with existing scheduling and weighting schemes. These findings establish instance-level noise valuation as a new axis for understanding and improving diffusion training. Code is available at https://github.com/JoeZhao527/Noise-Rater.

title: UniEvo-VL: An On-policy Self-Distillation Training Recipe for Multimodal Model Self-improvement
ss_tldr: UniEvo-VL, a self-evolving framework for multimodal models to learn from this constructive self-correction feedback during test-time compute, is introduced to enhance the user experience when using multimodal models without external supervision or guidance.
abstract: Modern multimodal models bring generation and understanding into a single unified system, which enables them to provide and learn from their own feedback. Motivated by this unified capacity, we introduce UniEvo-VL, a self-evolving framework for multimodal models to learn from this constructive self-correction feedback during test-time compute. Instead of relying on a separately trained, stronger generator as teacher, we use critiques of the generator's own outputs, produced by a fixed vision-language critic, as privileged information. The generator and its EMA copy act as student and teacher under different contexts. The student only sees the vanilla question, while the teacher conditions on the privileged critique. Then training minimizes the per-state divergence between their denoising diffusion distributions over the student's own sampling trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that UniEvo-VL improves the image generation capabilities of multimodal models, while maintaining their sensitivity to additional reflection information. With Qwen-Image-2512, direct-generation performance improves from 0.747 to 0.808 on GenEval using Qwen feedback and from 32.97 to 35.53 on GenEval2 Soft-TIFA using the external Luna critic. Moreover, attempts with more powerful external critics (e.g., GPT5.6-Luna) show that multimodal models with strong judge capabilities can anticipate a higher self-evolving ceiling. Last but not least, mixed text-rendering outcomes show that our self-improvements may not be uniform across different tasks. Our study aims to shed light on the current hot recursive self-improvement research line to enhance the user experience when using multimodal models without paired ground-truth images, human annotation, or task-specific reward functions.

title: Reconstruction Alignment Improves Unified Multimodal Models
ss_tldr: Reconstruction Alignment (RECA), a resource-efficient post-training method that leverages visual understanding encoder embeddings as dense"text prompts", providing rich supervision without captions, is introduced, establishing it as an efficient and general post-training alignment strategy for UMMs.
abstract: We discover a simple but effective way for visual understanding to help visual generation in a unified model. Unified multimodal models (UMMs) unify visual understanding and generation within a single architecture. However, conventional training relies on image-text pairs (or sequences) whose captions are typically sparse and miss fine-grained visual details, even when they use hundreds of words to describe a simple image. We introduce Reconstruction Alignment (RecA), a resource-efficient post-training method that leverages visual understanding encoder embeddings as dense "text prompts," providing rich supervision without captions. Concretely, RecA conditions a UMM on its own visual understanding embeddings and optimizes it to reconstruct the input image with a self-supervised reconstruction loss, thereby using visual understanding to improve image generation. Despite its simplicity, RecA is broadly applicable: across autoregressive, masked-autoregressive, and diffusion-based UMMs, it consistently improves generation and editing fidelity. With only 27 GPU hours, post-training with RecA substantially improves image generation performance on GenEval (0.73 $\rightarrow$ 0.90) and DPGBench (80.93 $\rightarrow$ 88.15), while also boosting editing benchmarks (ImgEdit 3.38 $\rightarrow$ 3.75, GEdit 6.94 $\rightarrow$ 7.27). Notably, RecA surpasses much larger open-source models and applies broadly across diverse UMM architectures, establishing it as an efficient and general post-training alignment strategy for UMMs.

title: Causality can systematically address the monsters under the bench(marks)
ss_tldr: It is argued causality offers an ideal framework to systematically address challenges of systematic evaluation and is demonstrated how the precise yet pragmatic language of causality clarifies the strengths and limitations of a method and inspires new approaches for systematic progress.
abstract: Effective and reliable evaluation is essential for advancing empirical machine learning. However, the increasing accessibility of generalist models and the progress towards ever more complex, high-level tasks make systematic evaluation more challenging. Benchmarks are plagued by various biases, artifacts, or leakage, while models may behave unreliably due to poorly explored failure modes. Haphazard treatments and inconsistent formulations of such "monsters" leads to a duplication of efforts, a lack of trust in results, and unsupported inferences. In this position paper, we argue causality offers an ideal framework to systematically address these challenges. By making causal assumptions in an approach explicit, we can faithfully model phenomena, formulate testable hypotheses with explanatory power, and leverage principled tools for analysis. To make the design of conceptual causal models more accessible, we identify several useful Common Abstract Topologies (CATs) in causal graphs which help gain insight into the reasoning abilities in large language models. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate how the precise yet pragmatic language of causality clarifies the strengths and limitations of a method and inspires new approaches for systematic progress.

title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
abstract: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

title: Depth-Linked Residual Tokens for Multimodal Retrieval and Generation
abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.

title: Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale
ss_tldr: This work highlights the difference between quick agentic turnaround times and the minutes-long user idle periods at turn boundaries, and designs a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 86-90\% of total idle time, enabling proactive decisions for efficient resource orchestration.
abstract: AI coding agents (e.g., GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex) interleave multi-step LLM inference with tool execution, creating a workload different from chatbots. We present the first production-scale characterization of coding agents using sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June-July 2026, comprising 7.4M users, 819M conversations, 5.7B LLM calls, and 946T tokens. Our analysis reveals distinctive workload properties with unique systems implications: e.g., sparse user-initiated turns unfold into autonomous agent loops with nearly 1:1 coupling between LLM calls and tool execution; parallel LLM calls are rare but exist in turns that trigger subagents; KV cache hit rates average 90% within a turn, but fall to 52% across turn boundaries and to 6% after model switches; workflows and user behaviors exhibit diverse, long-tailed resource footprints. We further distinguish short agentic turnaround times from minutes-long user idle periods between turns, and develop a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 87-89% of total idle time. We demonstrate two use cases: (1) a harness-side LLM API keep-alive policy that preserves provider-side context KV cache, reducing token costs by 14.9% on turn boundaries; and (2) a serving-side KV cache residency policy that uses predicted idle time to guide DRAM offloading, reducing time to first token (TTFT) by 3-33% compared with LRU during a one-week evaluation with GitHub Copilot traces.

title: Unifying matrix completion across domains with a synthetically pretrained foundation model
abstract: Matrix completion underlies problems from tabular imputation to causal inference. While matrix completion provides a common setup for these domains, the best methods in each domain are still specialized and do not transfer well across domains. We introduce MatrixFormer, a pre-trained matrix-native transformer that predicts a full distribution for every missing entry in a single forward pass. MatrixFormer is trained entirely on synthetic low-rank and latent-factor matrices under diverse missingness patterns. Applied zero-shot with fixed network weights, MatrixFormer achieves competitive performance on causal inference panel-data tasks, tabular imputation, and recommendation systems matrix completion. These results position MatrixFormer as a general-purpose foundation model for matrix completion.

title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
ss_tldr: MAWAM is introduced, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample and shows that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control.
abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

title: RAG Makes Guardrails Brittle? Investigating Robustness of Guardrails under RAG-style Contexts
ss_tldr: It is confirmed that inserting benign documents into the guardrail context alters the judgments of input and output guardrails in around 11% and 8% of cases, making them unreliable.
abstract: With the increasing adoption of large language models (LLMs), ensuring the safety of LLM systems has become a pressing concern. External LLM-based guardrail models have emerged as a popular solution to screen unsafe inputs and outputs, but they are themselves fine-tuned or prompt-engineered LLMs vulnerable to data distribution shifts. In this paper, taking Retrieval Augmentation Generation (RAG) as a case study, we investigate how robust LLM-based guardrails are against additional information embedded in the context. Through a systematic evaluation of 3 Llama Guards and 2 GPT-oss models, we find that inserting benign retrieved documents flips the judgments of input and output guardrails in around 11% and 8% of cases respectively, with the majority of these flips (72% and 64%) reversing previously correct decisions. We further analyze the effect of each component in the augmented context: retrieved documents, user query, and LLM response. Two tested mitigations reveal that the robustness gap is not easily closed. These results expose a context-robustness gap in current guardrails.

title: Preserving Pretrained CFG Structure in RL for Diffusion Models with Conditional Contrast Regularization
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.

title: EgoPhys: Physics-Informed Digital Twins for Deformable Objects from Egocentric Video
ss_tldr: EgoPhys overcomes the limitations of existing methods to enable controllable deformable digital twin generation from egocentric videos by distilling per-object inverse-physics solutions into a compact codebook, enabling prediction of dense spring stiffness fields for unseen objects without per-spring test-time optimization.
abstract: Humans naturally understand object physics through everyday interactions, but predicting how deformable objects, such as soft objects and fabrics, respond to manipulation remains a major challenge for computer vision and robotics. Existing deformable physical twin methods typically rely on controlled multi-view or depth capture and costly per-object physical refinement. We present EgoPhys, a framework for constructing predictive deformable physical twins from a single egocentric RGB interaction. EgoPhys combines persistent correspondences with per-frame monocular 3D observations to fit a sequence-specific spring-mass model from moving-camera observations. Because a short interaction weakly constrains fine-grained local stiffness, EgoPhys amortizes this refinement across training interactions using a compact state-conditioned residual model that predicts bounded local corrections around the sequence-specific estimate and remains frozen at test time. Experiments show improved held-out future prediction over adapted deformable-twin baselines, with the amortized residual further improving prediction while reducing local-refinement cost by approximately 10-59x over dense per-spring optimization. The resulting twins also support deformable-object action selection, with representative physical robot manipulation providing a qualitative proof of concept.

title: SYSEVOLVE: Safe, Autonomous Attack-Defense Co-evolution for Evolving Cyber Defense
abstract: The offensive capability of large language models (LLMs) has crossed from research demonstration into documented reality. Frontier models have autonomously breached real production systems, and open-weight models now deliver frontier-level exploitation at negligible cost. Existing defenses cannot keep pace with such attacks: human-intensive defense updates over days to weeks, while AI-based defense, on the other side, trained on fixed historical data, does not adapt to an evolving attacker. We trace these persistent failures to one root cause: defense evolves in isolation, cut off from the adversary that should be driving its evolution. That isolation manifests at three layers: the deployment layer, the capability layer, and the adversarial layer. To build a defense that evolves at the speed of attack, we propose co-evolution as the integrating insight, replacing isolated evolution with mutual driving between attack and defense. Based on this insight, we present SysEvolve, a safe and autonomous co-evolutionary system built from three co-designed components, SysField, SysSpear, and SysArmor. SysField constructs realistic multi-host ranges via declarative topology-driven construction. SysSpear generates efficient, safe attack schemes via task-sliced local search, a bidirectional expert-knowledge base, and static-analysis verification. SysArmor performs real-time, interpretable defense via state tracking, CTI-context fusion, and stage-matched response. In evaluation, SysField achieves zero-loss collection at 2.1\% overhead and orchestrates 257 CVEs into 1,148 ranges. SysSpear improves red-team success by over 25\%, attains the best completion on complex multi-vulnerability ranges. SysArmor achieves 10--1000$\times$ greater precision than prior systems and detects real APT attacks in production at Huawei and Sangfor. Our evaluation also reveals four findings about LLM agent capabilities.

title: PiXTime: A Model for Federated Time Series Forecasting with Heterogeneous Data across Nodes
ss_tldr: Comprehensive evaluations on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PiXTime achieves state-of-the-art performance in heterogeneous federated environments, while maintaining robust superiority in standard homogeneous and centralized forecasting settings.
abstract: While collaborative forecasting on distributed time series is highly desirable, directly pooling localized datasets is often impractical due to data sharing constraints. Federated learning offers a promising alternative, yet conventional federated learning algorithms require homogeneous model architectures, which are incompatible with the structural discrepancies, such as unaligned temporal resolutions and mismatched variable channels, commonly observed across decentralized nodes. To bridge this gap, we introduce PiXTime, a novel Transformer-based framework designed to natively accommodate and leverage structurally heterogeneous temporal data. At its core, PiXTime adopts a parameter-decoupling architecture, strategically partitioning the model into localized personalized modules and a globally aggregated shared backbone. Specifically, node-specific local modules act as dimensional adapters, projecting raw sequences of diverse lengths into a unified representation space. Concurrently, a globally synchronized VE Table injects consistent categorical identities into the feature space, allowing the shared backbone to collaboratively learn and generalize representations across inconsistent variable distributions. Comprehensive evaluations on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PiXTime achieves state-of-the-art performance in heterogeneous federated environments, while maintaining robust superiority in standard homogeneous and centralized forecasting settings.

title: Agentic programs: an emerging form of scientific software in computational materials science
ss_tldr: It is argued that recent LLM-based agent harnesses enable an emerging form of scientific software, agentic programs, that combine deterministic algorithms with bounded LLM-based judgment, task-specific verification, episodic maturation, and complete delegation in production.
abstract: Computational materials science has traditionally delegated algorithmic tasks to computers while leaving scientific judgments to humans. In this Perspective, we argue that agent harnesses built on large language models (LLMs) enable an emerging form of scientific software, agentic programs, integrating deterministic algorithms with bounded LLM-based judgment, task-specific verification, episodic maturation, and complete delegation. We illustrate these characteristics through DeMARS, which constructs atomistic models from experimentally measured disordered crystal structures.

title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
